etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English litterate, from Latin līterātus, litterātus. Doublet of literato and literatus.

definitions.definition: Able to read and write; having literacy.

quote.citation: 1997, George Carlin, Brain Droppings‎[1], New York: Hyperion Books, →ISBN, →LCCN, →OCLC, →OL, page 86:
quote.text: Intelligence tests are biased toward the literate.

definitions.definition: Knowledgeable in literature, writing; literary; well-read.

quote.citation: 2008 January 7, Charles Hugh Smith, Can a Fragmented Culture Find Common Ground?‎[2]:
quote.text: The reason literature plays a unique role in any literate culture is its longevity.

definitions.definition: Which is used in writing (of a language or dialect).

quote.citation: 2005, Nicholas Ostler, Empires of the Word: A Language History of the World, Harper:
quote.text: The Mongol emperor Kublai Khan even commissioned an alphabetic script for his empire, to be used officially for all its literate languages, Mongolian, Chinese, Turkic and Persian.

definitions.definition: A person who is able to read and write.
(historical) A person who was educated but had not taken a university degree; especially a candidate to take holy orders.
